title: Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host
content:
## 1.3 Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host

FIELDWISE is a European Fellowship: the experienced researcher Dr. Rositsa Cholakova moves intra-EU from Bulgaria to the host beneficiary, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) in Hungary, for a 30-month action comprising a 24-month fellowship at ELTE (M1–M24) and a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR (M25–M30). Because it is a European Fellowship, the relevant transfer-of-knowledge test under this criterion is the two-way transfer between the researcher and the host; the three-way transfer required of Global Fellowships (researcher, host, and associated partner for an outgoing phase) does not apply, and no separate secondment is included in this action — the only inter-sectoral mobility is the non-academic placement described in §1.3.4.

## 1.3.1 Qualifications and experience of the supervisory team

Supervision is delivered by a complementary two-person team at the beneficiary, chosen so that the disciplinary reach of the supervision matches the interdisciplinary object of the fellowship — the interface of crop physiology and geospatial data science set out in §1.1 and §1.2. Overall scientific supervision is provided by Prof. András Jung, Professor at ELTE's Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, whose expertise is in remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, field spectroscopy, geospatial technologies and environmental monitoring. This is precisely the competence base on which the hyperspectral early-warning and hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer methodology of WP2 (Physiological Early Warning and Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel Transfer) depends; it is also directly served by the institute's own hyperspectral instrumentation (the Ultris S5 and Cubert CUVIS Lab Lite in its GIS and Remote Sensing Laboratory). Prof. András Jung chairs the Project Steering Group and is the fellow's primary supervisor and the escalation point for scientific method.

Methodological co-supervision is provided by Dr. Roland Hollós (ORCID 0000-0001-5137-7471) of ELTE's Department of Meteorology, whose expertise is in machine learning and meta-modelling of crop and grassland multi-model outputs and in agro-meteorology. He holds the methodological lead and the quality assurance for model development and testing across WP3 (Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction) and WP4 (Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability): the fellow designs, builds and runs the models, while the co-supervisor quality-assures the modelling strategy and the leakage-safe validation design that is the backbone of the honest-estimate methodology. His supervision under the action is carried out at the beneficiary, and because the two supervisors sit in different ELTE departments, the supervision is itself interdisciplinary within the host institution — a Bayesian/uncertainty-aware modelling strand alongside the remote-sensing strand. A third, informal scientific-advisory strand is contributed by Prof. Gábor Milics of Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem (MATE), a full professor and Hungary's country representative to the International Society of Precision Agriculture, who advises the fellow personally on remote sensing in precision agriculture (a role he held in the predecessor proposal and continues for FIELDWISE) without occupying a governance seat.

On track record and experience in supervising and training at advanced level, two points are stated with deliberate candour rather than embellishment, consistent with the evaluation framework's status discipline. First, the professorial standing of Prof. András Jung establishes his capacity to supervise at doctoral and postdoctoral level, and the fellow–supervisor pairing is not untested: ELTE hosted a prior MSCA-PF application, PLANTDIGISENSE (HORIZON-MSCA-2025-PF, proposal 101284764), with the same fellow and the same supervisor, which scored 70.40% against a 70.00 threshold. FIELDWISE is therefore a strengthened resubmission by an established pairing that has already worked together on an MSCA-PF proposal at this host, not a first collaboration. Second, and in the same spirit of transparency, ELTE has not previously hosted a funded MSCA fellow (this is recorded as an operator-declared assumption, not as evidence), and the institute's detailed recent-project, publication and doctoral-supervision record is a host-capacity item that only the participating organisation can supply; it is therefore developed in Part B-1 §3.2 rather than asserted here, so that the evaluator can see where the confirmed supervision arrangements end and the host-capacity detail begins.

## 1.3.2 Planned training activities for the researcher

Training is structured around a Career Development Plan (deliverable D1.3, Career Development Plan, due month 3), established jointly by the supervisors and the researcher and signed by both supervisors and the fellow — the joint establishment the call mandates, read as "both supervisors" because a co-supervisor is in place. The plan is agreed early in the action and reviewed at five governance points (M6, M12, M16, M20 and M27), the M27 review falling inside the placement window precisely so that non-academic career development is monitored when it is most in play. The plan spans research objectives (O1–O6), training and career needs, transferable skills, teaching, publications planning and open-science engagement, and it is the instrument through which the three training strands below are sequenced and reviewed.

**Scientific and technical training (host → fellow).** The host delivers eleven target competences as supervised research practice embedded across WP2–WP5 plus named ELTE courses: geoinformatics; EO time-series analysis; optical/SAR integration; hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer; spatio-temporal modelling; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; uncertainty quantification; transfer learning/domain adaptation; reproducible geospatial computation; research software/web deployment; and IP and research exploitation. These map directly onto the fellow's stated competence gap (Bayesian/probabilistic modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor-domain transfer, uncertainty, cross-country adaptation and decision evaluation) and onto the intended progression from Plant Physiologist/Agronomist to EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist to an independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence.

**Transferable and management skills.** Seven transferable-skill strands are trained: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication. This satisfies the call's requirement (SR-04) that training integrate key transferable skills — expressly including digital skills such as generative AI — and foster an Open Science culture, knowledge valorisation and good scientific conduct including research integrity. Management competence is trained concretely rather than nominally: the fellow runs the work plan, keeps a monthly written progress record, and sits in the Project Steering Group, gaining first-hand project-management and coordination experience across an academic–research–industry consortium.

**Teaching and education.** Two teaching measures feed research results back into host teaching: co-designing and delivering a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture (rather than a single guest lecture), and co-supervising the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work. In the Career Development Plan the teaching component is framed not as a competence to be acquired but as an existing strength — five years of syllabus design, lecturing and examining at Agricultural University Plovdiv (2015–2020) in Bulgarian and English, with Bachelor's thesis supervision — transferred to a new discipline, a new institution and a new language of instruction, and stepped up from Bachelor's to doctoral-level supervision.

**Publications and public engagement.** The plan targets four principal scientific outputs (P1–P4) with at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship, one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers, and one public-facing article per year. This supervision-and-training design cadences the fellow's development: a weekly one-to-one with the supervisor, a weekly technical session with the co-supervisor through WP3 and WP4 (M6–M21) tapering to monthly outside that window, a monthly written progress record, and a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors.

## 1.3.3 Two-way transfer of knowledge between researcher and host

The transfer of knowledge is genuinely bidirectional, and it is constitutive of the science rather than a courtesy: the physiological target defines what the geospatial model must predict, and the geospatial-modelling apparatus determines which physiological signatures can be scaled and forecast. From host to fellow, ELTE transfers the eleven geospatial and data-science competences listed in §1.3.2. From fellow to host, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova brings the plant-science foundation the host's remote-sensing and meteorology groups do not themselves hold: plant physiology; horticultural crop science; plant protection/agronomy; water-stress experimentation; physiological phenotyping; hyperspectral field measurements; biological interpretation of Earth-observation signals; the preliminary development of the DrR - Digital Agronomist prototype; and access to complementary agricultural research collaborations. The net exchange is crop physiology/agronomy ↔ geospatial/data science — the two disciplinary bases that §1.2 integrates into a single method — and it directly serves the call's expected outcomes on stronger R&I capacity and better knowledge transfer among participating organisations (EO-07) and on enhanced quality and sustainability of research training and supervision at the host (EO-05).

Although the formal European-Fellowship requirement concerns the researcher and the host only, the associated partners enrich this exchange into an academic–research–industry knowledge chain without altering where the two-way obligation sits. Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem (MATE) contributes long-term experimental and physiological knowledge and the source-domain dataset for model development and validation; Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив (MVCRI) contributes the independent Bulgarian research environment for the Hungary→Bulgaria cross-country transferability test (a true geographic transfer, not merely a larger sample); and AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság contributes the bridge from research field to farmer field and from research prototype to operational requirements. The fellow is the connective tissue of this chain, carrying physiological understanding into a geoinformatics faculty and geospatial-prediction competence back out toward operational agriculture.

## 1.3.4 Rationale and added value of the non-academic placement

The action includes an optional non-academic sector placement, permitted under the call (SR-06) as up to six additional months at the end of the fellowship in a non-academic organisation established in an EU Member State, and required to be an integral, explicitly justified and evaluated part of the proposal. AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság (a private for-profit SME in Budaörs, Hungary, operating a commercial farm management information system used across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria) hosts the placement over the final six months of the 30-month action (M25–M30). The company co-leads WP5 (Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP) from earlier in the action and then hosts the fellow on site, so the placement deepens existing WP5 content rather than introducing a new strand.

**Added value for the project.** The placement makes the operational-transfer half of the proposal structural rather than asserted. Gap G5 and hypothesis H5 both claim that research-to-farm transfer is where locally developed agricultural models break; a six-month period embedded inside the company that runs the farms is the strongest available evidence that the proposal takes its own thesis seriously, and it directly answers the previous evaluation's recorded criticism that the economic and technological route to users was insufficiently substantiated. **Added value for the researcher's career.** The placement supplies the inter-sectoral half of the intended career progression — operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and direct exposure to commercial agricultural-software requirements — none of which the academic host can provide, and it is the segment of the profile that makes the fellow employable in precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and FMIS companies as well as in academia. **Why it must be inside the company and why it needs six months.** The concrete work content of the placement depends on the company's own production environment and its customer-facing requirements: operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production FMIS environment; the nine-dimension operational assessment producing D5.4 (AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation, due month 30); the FMIS integration roadmap written from inside the implementing company, producing D5.5 (FMIS integration roadmap, due month 30); and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers. So that the placement is validation and transfer rather than first build, the web MVP is delivered before the placement begins as D5.1 (DrR web MVP, due month 24). The fellow is supervised on site by Miklós Maróti, senior research officer at the company — a research-grade supervisory register appropriate to the placement's training rationale — with a working desk/office location and access to the company's FMIS development/staging and customer-data environments for the six months; these on-site hosting facts rest on operator declarations about AgroVIR's own staff and facilities and are recorded as assumptions to be confirmed with the company, in line with the honest sourcing applied throughout this proposal. In accordance with the Guide for Applicants, the placement is described here in Part B-1 for assessment under this criterion, no letter of commitment is included for the non-academic placement host, and the six-month ceiling is used in full.
